s: clothes should not be accepted very expensive (including fur, fine, beautiful, and specified costly materials)
q: A monk or a nun should not accept any very expensive clothes of the following description: clothes made of fur, fine ones, beautiful ones; clothes made of goats' hair, of blue cotton, of common cotton, of Bengal cotton, of Patta, of Malaya fibres, of bark fibres, of muslin, of silk; (clothes provincially called) Desaraga, Amila, Gaggala, Phâliya, Kâyaha; blankets or mantles.

s: clothes begging rules is a four rules (for begging clothes)
q: For the avoidance of these occasions to sin there are four rules for begging clothes to be known by the mendicants.

s: clothes begging rules include inspection of a robe (as the second rule)
q: A monk or a nun may ask for clothes which they have well inspected, from the householder or his wife, &c.

s: clothes begging rules include borrowing a robe (as a prohibited practice addressed in the second lesson)
q: 'Well, I shall borrow a robe and return after staying abroad for one, two, three, four, or five days; perhaps it will thus become my own.' As this would be sinful, he should not do so.

s: householder may offer promise to provide clothes (for a future time)
q: O long-lived Sramana! return after a month, ten nights, five nights, to-morrow, to-morrow night; then we shall give you some clothes.'

s: monk should not accept promise to provide clothes (should request clothes immediately)
q: it is not meet for me to accept such a promise. If you want to give me (something), give it me now!'

s: householder is a giver of clothes (to a mendicant)
q: If they beg for them, or the householder gives them, they may accept them; for they are pure and acceptable.

s: Kevalin states the reason for inspecting a robe (because it may contain hidden things or living matter)
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason: There might be hidden in the robe an earring or girdle or gold and silver, &c. (see II, 2, 1, § 11), or living beings or seeds or grass.

s: inspection of a robe is required for clothes (inspection of the inside before acceptance)
q: Hence it has been said to the mendicant, &c., that he should closely inspect the inside of the robe.

s: clothes should not be washed or dyed washing and dyeing clothes (because they are not new)
q: A monk or a nun should not wash his clothes, rub or wipe them with ground drugs, &c., because they are not new.

s: washing and dyeing clothes is prohibited clothes (for clothes that are not new)
q: A monk or a nun should not wash his clothes, rub or wipe them with ground drugs, &c., because they are not new.

s: airing or drying clothes should be done on heap of ashes or bones (in a secluded spot after repeated inspection and cleaning)
q: Knowing this, he should resort to a secluded spot, and circumspectly air or dry his clothes there on a heap of ashes or bones, &c. (see II, 1, 1, § 1), which he has repeatedly inspected and cleaned.

s: First Lesson concerns clothes (begging and use)
q: Fifth Lecture, Called Begging of Clothes. First Lesson.

s: airing or drying clothes should not be done on bare ground (or wet earth, rock, or living clay)
q: A monk or a nun wanting to air or dry (in the sun) their clothes, should not do so on the bare ground or wet earth or rock or piece of clay containing life, &c. (see II, 1, 5, § 2).

s: airing or drying clothes should not be done on abode of a householder (including unstable above-ground places)
q: A monk or a nun wanting to air or dry (in the sun) their clothes, should not hang them for that purpose on a post of a house, on the upper timber of a door-frame, on a mortar, on a bathing-tub, or on any such-like above-ground place, which is not well fixed or set, but shaky and movable.

s: monk should wear clothes (in the state in which they are received)
q: A monk or a nun should beg for acceptable clothes, and wear them in that state in which they get them;

s: nun should wear clothes (in the state in which they are received)
q: A monk or a nun should beg for acceptable clothes, and wear them in that state in which they get them;

s: monk should be outfitted with clothes (when entering a householder's abode for alms)
q: A monk or a nun wanting, for the sake of alms, to enter the abode of a householder, should do so outfitted with all their clothes;

s: nun should be outfitted with clothes (when entering a householder's abode for alms)
q: A monk or a nun wanting, for the sake of alms, to enter the abode of a householder, should do so outfitted with all their clothes;

s: monk should not enter or leave abode of a householder (for alms during strong and widely spread rain)
q: A monk or a nun dressed in all their clothes should not enter or leave, for the sake of alms, the abode of a householder, &c. &c., on perceiving that a strong and widely spread rain pours down, &c. (see II, 1, 3, § 9).

s: nun should not enter or leave abode of a householder (for alms during strong and widely spread rain)
q: A monk or a nun dressed in all their clothes should not enter or leave, for the sake of alms, the abode of a householder, &c. &c., on perceiving that a strong and widely spread rain pours down, &c. (see II, 1, 3, § 9).

s: thieves desire clothes (when encountered on a forest road)
q: If the road of a monk or a nun on the pilgrimage lies through a forest in which, as they know, there stroll bands of many thieves desirous of their clothes,

s: Second Lesson concerns clothes (wearing and protection)
q: Second Lesson. A monk or a nun should beg for acceptable clothes, and wear them in that state in which they get them; they should not wash or dye them, nor should they wear washed or dyed clothes, nor (should they) hide (their clothes) when passing through other villages, being careless of dress.

s: monk should not leave road (from fear of thieves or to save clothes)
q: If he sees in his way thieves, he should not from fear of them, and to save his clothes, leave the road or go into another road,

s: pilgrimage may pass through forest (when the road lies through it despite thieves)
q: If the road of a monk or a nun on the pilgrimage lies through a forest in which, as they know, there stroll bands of many thieves desirous of their clothes,

s: monk may beg for cloth made of wool, silk, hemp, palm-leaves, cotton, or Arkatûla
q: A monk or a nun wanting to get clothes, may beg for cloth made of wool, silk, hemp, palm-leaves, cotton, or Arkatûla, or such-like clothes.

s: nun may beg for cloth made of wool, silk, hemp, palm-leaves, cotton, or Arkatûla
q: A monk or a nun wanting to get clothes, may beg for cloth made of wool, silk, hemp, palm-leaves, cotton, or Arkatûla, or such-like clothes.

s: monk may wear one robe (if youthful, young, strong, healthy, and well-set)
q: If he be a youthful, young, strong, healthy, well-set monk, he may wear one robe, not two;

s: nun should possess four raiments (one two cubits broad, two three cubits broad, and one four cubits broad)
q: if a nun, she should possess four raiments, one two cubits broad, two three cubits broad, one four cubits broad.

s: Begging for a Bowl is a lecture
q: Sixth Lecture, Called Begging for a Bowl.

s: alms-bowl may be made of clay
q: A monk or a nun wanting to get a bowl, may beg for one made of bottle-gourd or wood or clay, or such-like bowls.

s: monk should not accept alms-bowl (bought by the householder for the mendicant's sake)
q: A monk or a nun should not accept a bowl which the layman has, for the mendicant's sake, bought, &c. (see the Lecture called Begging of Clothes). (I

s: nun should not accept alms-bowl (bought by the householder for the mendicant's sake)
q: A monk or a nun should not accept a bowl which the layman has, for the mendicant's sake, bought, &c. (see the Lecture called Begging of Clothes). (I

s: alms-bowl is unacceptable very expensive (when made of the listed precious materials)
q: A monk or a nun should not accept any very expensive bowls of the following description: bowls made of iron, tin, lead, silver, gold, brass, a mixture of gold, silver, and copper, pearl, glass, mother of pearl, horn, ivory, cloth, stone, or leather; for such very expensive bowls are impure and unacceptable. (2)

s: alms-bowl is impure very expensive (when made of the listed precious materials)
q: A monk or a nun should not accept any very expensive bowls of the following description: bowls made of iron, tin, lead, silver, gold, brass, a mixture of gold, silver, and copper, pearl, glass, mother of pearl, horn, ivory, cloth, stone, or leather; for such very expensive bowls are impure and unacceptable. (2)

s: alms-bowl may be used by many people (when previously used)
q: A monk or a nun may beg for a bowl which has been used by the former owner or by many people.

s: alms-bowl may be left off Sramanas (when no Sramana, Brâhmana, guest, pauper, or beggar wants it)
q: A monk or a nun may beg for a left-off bowl which no other Sramana or Brâhmana, guest, pauper, or beggar wants.

s: householder may give alms-bowl (to a monk or nun begging in the prescribed way)
q: A householder may perhaps say to a mendicant begging in the prescribed way: 'O long-lived Sramana! return after a month,' &c. (all as in the Lecture called Begging of Clothes). (8)

s: monk should inspect alms-bowl (closely inspecting its interior before acceptance)
q: Perhaps the householder will bring and give the mendicant an alms-bowl; the mendicant should then, after consideration, say: 'O long-lived one! (or, O sister!) I shall in your presence closely inspect the interior of the bowl.'

s: alms-bowl may contain living beings
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason: In the alms-bowl there might be living beings or seeds or grass.

s: monk may carry one bowl (if youthful)
q: If he be a youthful, young, &c. (see II, 5, 1, § 1) monk, he may carry with him one bowl, not two.

s: alms-bowl may contain seeds
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason: In the alms-bowl there might be living beings or seeds or grass.

s: alms-bowl may contain grass
q: The Kevalin says: This is the reason: In the alms-bowl there might be living beings or seeds or grass.

s: monk should enter or leave householder's abode (after examining the alms-bowl, removing living beings, and wiping off dust)
q: A monk or a nun, entering the abode of a householder for the sake of alms, should after examining their alms-bowl, taking out any living beings, and wiping off the dust, circumspectly enter or leave the householder's abode.

s: nun should enter or leave householder's abode (after examining the alms-bowl, removing living beings, and wiping off dust)
q: A monk or a nun, entering the abode of a householder for the sake of alms, should after examining their alms-bowl, taking out any living beings, and wiping off the dust, circumspectly enter or leave the householder's abode.

s: alms-bowl is unacceptable filled with cold water (when offered by the householder)
q: On such an occasion the householder might perhaps, going in the house, fill the alms-bowl with cold water and, returning, offer it him; (the mendicant) should not accept such an alms-bowl either in the householder's hand or his vessel; for it is impure and unacceptable. (2)

s: monk should not wipe or rub alms-bowl (when wet or moist)
q: A monk or a nun should not wipe or rub a wet or moist alms-bowl.

s: nun should not wipe or rub alms-bowl (when wet or moist)
q: A monk or a nun should not wipe or rub a wet or moist alms-bowl.

s: monk may wipe or rub alms-bowl (when the water has dried up and the moisture is gone)
q: But when they perceive that on their alms-bowl the water has dried up and the moisture is gone, then they may circumspectly wipe or rub it.

s: nun may wipe or rub alms-bowl (when the water has dried up and the moisture is gone)
q: But when they perceive that on their alms-bowl the water has dried up and the moisture is gone, then they may circumspectly wipe or rub it.

s: monk should carry alms-bowl (when entering or leaving a householder's abode for alms)
q: A monk or a nun wanting to enter the abode of a householder, should enter or leave it, for the sake of alms, with their bowl; also on going to the out-of-door place for religious practices or study; or on wandering from village to village.

s: nun should carry alms-bowl (when entering or leaving a householder's abode for alms)
q: A monk or a nun wanting to enter the abode of a householder, should enter or leave it, for the sake of alms, with their bowl; also on going to the out-of-door place for religious practices or study; or on wandering from village to village.

s: monk should protect alms-bowl (during strong and widely spread rain as prescribed for clothes)
q: If a strong and widely spread rain pours down, they should take the same care of their alms-bowl as is prescribed for clothes (in the preceding Lecture, Lesson 2, § 1).

s: nun should protect alms-bowl (during strong and widely spread rain as prescribed for clothes)
q: If a strong and widely spread rain pours down, they should take the same care of their alms-bowl as is prescribed for clothes (in the preceding Lecture, Lesson 2, § 1).

s: monk should not go farther than half a Yogana (to get a bowl)
q: A monk or a nun should not resolve to go farther than half a Yogana to get a bowl.

s: nun should not go farther than half a Yogana (to get a bowl)
q: A monk or a nun should not resolve to go farther than half a Yogana to get a bowl.

s: monk may beg for alms-bowl (made of bottle-gourd, wood, or clay)
q: A monk or a nun may beg for a bowl specifying its quality, viz. bottle-gourd or wood or clay.

s: nun may beg for alms-bowl (made of bottle-gourd, wood, or clay)
q: A monk or a nun may beg for a bowl specifying its quality, viz. bottle-gourd or wood or clay.

s: alms-bowl may be made of bottle-gourd
q: A monk or a nun wanting to get a bowl, may beg for one made of bottle-gourd or wood or clay, or such-like bowls.

s: alms-bowl may be made of wood
q: A monk or a nun wanting to get a bowl, may beg for one made of bottle-gourd or wood or clay, or such-like bowls.

s: Seventh Lecture, Called Regulation of Possession is a lecture
q: Seventh Lecture, Called Regulation of Possession.

s: Sramanas takes possession of traveller's hall (only with permission of the landlord or steward)
q: He may beg for a domicile in a traveller's hall, &c. (see II, 1, 8, § 2), having reflected (on its fitness for a stay); he should ask permission to take possession of it from him who is the landlord or the steward of that place

s: fellow-ascetic is a zealous brother
q: Having got possession of some place, a mendicant should invite to that food, &c., which he himself has collected, any fellow-ascetics arriving there who follow the same rules and are zealous brethren

s: fellow-ascetic follows same rules (when receiving food collected by a mendicant)
q: Having got possession of some place, a mendicant should invite to that food, &c., which he himself has collected, any fellow-ascetics arriving there who follow the same rules and are zealous brethren

s: fellow-ascetic follows other rules (when offered a footstool, bench, bed, or couch)
q: Having got possession of some place (in a traveller's hall, &c.), a mendicant should offer a footstool or bench or bed or couch, which he himself has begged, to any fellow-ascetics arriving there who follow other rules than he, yet are zealous brethren

s: householder has dominion householder's dominion
q: The houseowner's dominion; The householder's dominion;

s: householder grants permission for possession (as landlord or steward of a place)
q: he should ask permission to take possession of it from him who is the landlord or the steward of that place: 'Indeed, O long-lived one! for the time, and in the space which you concede us, we shall dwell here

s: traveller's hall is a domicile (a place where mendicants may stay with permission)
q: He may beg for a domicile in a traveller's hall, &c. (see II, 1, 8, § 2), having reflected (on its fitness for a stay)

s: mango is impure covered with eggs and living beings (when perceived in that condition)
q: If the monk or the nun perceive that the mango is covered with eggs, living beings, &c. (see II, 1, 1, § 2), they should not take it; for it is impure, &c.

s: mango is pure nibbled at by animals and injured (when free from eggs and living beings)
q: But if they perceive that the mango is free from eggs, living beings, &c., and is nibbled at by animals and injured, then they may take it; for it is pure, &c.

s: mango has parts peel
q: The monk might wish to eat or suck one half of a mango or a mango's peel or rind or sap or smaller particles.

s: mango has parts rind
q: The monk might wish to eat or suck one half of a mango or a mango's peel or rind or sap or smaller particles.

s: mango has parts sap
q: The monk might wish to eat or suck one half of a mango or a mango's peel or rind or sap or smaller particles.

s: dominion is a fivefold classification (as declared by the Sthaviras)
q: The Sthaviras, the venerable ones, have declared that dominion is fivefold:

s: dominion includes the lord of the gods' dominion
q: The lord of the gods' dominion;

s: dominion includes the king's dominion
q: The king's dominion;

s: dominion includes the houseowner's dominion
q: The houseowner's dominion;

s: dominion includes the householder's dominion
q: The householder's dominion;

s: dominion includes the religious man's dominion
q: The religious man's dominion.

s: The Venerable Ascetic Mahâvîra explains dominion (through the following explanation)
q: I have heard the following explanation by the venerable (Mahâvîra): The Sthaviras, the venerable ones, have declared that dominion is fivefold:

s: seven rules of possession is a seven rules (for occupying a dwelling-place)
q: Now follows the seventh rule:

s: Sramanas owns no house (under vows of renunciation)
q: 'I shall become a Sramana who owns no house, no property, no sons, no cattle, who eats what others give him; I shall commit no sinful action; Master, I renounce to accept anything that has not been given.'

s: seven rules of possession includes asking for a domicile after reflecting on its fitness (first rule)
q: Now this is the first rule: He may beg for a domicile in a traveller's hall, &c., having reflected (on its fitness for a stay), &c. (§ 2 of the preceding Lesson is to be repeated here).

s: seven rules of possession includes taking possession for other mendicants and using the dwelling-place (second rule)
q: A monk resolves: 'I shall ask for possession of a dwelling-place, &c., for the sake of other mendicants, and having taken possession of it for their sake, I shall use it.'

s: seven rules of possession includes taking possession for other mendicants without using the dwelling-place (third rule)
q: A monk resolves: 'I shall ask for possession of a dwelling-place, &c., for the sake of other mendicants, and having taken possession of it for their sake, I shall not use it.'

s: seven rules of possession includes using a dwelling-place ceded to other mendicants (fourth rule)
q: A monk resolves: 'I shall not ask for possession of a dwelling-place, &c., for the sake of other mendicants; but if the dwelling-place, &c., has already been ceded to them, I shall use it.'

s: seven rules of possession includes asking for a dwelling-place for one's own sake (fifth rule; not for two, three, four, or five persons)
q: A monk resolves: 'I shall ask for possession of a dwelling-place for my own sake, not for two, three, four, or five persons.'

s: seven rules of possession includes using Ikkada reed when obtained in a dwelling-place (sixth rule)
q: If a monk or a nun, occupying a dwelling-place in which there is Ikkada reed, &c. (see II, 2, 3, § 18), get this thing, then they may use it; otherwise they should remain in a squatting or sitting posture.

s: seven rules of possession includes using a clay-paved dwelling-place when obtained (seventh rule)
q: A monk or a nun may beg for a dwelling-place paved with clay or wood. If they get it, then they may use it; otherwise they should remain in a squatting or sitting posture.

s: Sramanas owns no property (under vows of renunciation)
q: 'I shall become a Sramana who owns no house, no property, no sons, no cattle, who eats what others give him; I shall commit no sinful action; Master, I renounce to accept anything that has not been given.'

s: Sramanas is a mendicant
q: Having taken such vows, (a mendicant) should not, on entering a village or scot-free town, &c., take himself, or induce others to take, or allow others to take, what has not been given.

q: Ninth Lecture.

s: place for study is pure and acceptable (if that place for study is free from eggs or living beings)
q: But if that place for study to which they wish to go, is free from eggs or living beings, &c., they may accept it; for it is pure and acceptable.

s: place for study is acceptable acceptable (when free from eggs or living beings)

q: Tenth Lecture.

s: monk should not ease nature on appropriated place (when the householder kills living beings or commits sins for ascetics)
